body.text: On the banks of Powai Lake, on the outskirts of Sanjay Gandhi National Park, IIT Bombay has a picturesque location. Entering the campus itself gives the impression that it is one of India’s premier higher educational institutions. It is. No wonder Sahil Wakode wanted to crack the JEE and enter the campus. He was 22 when he died by suicide on September 18.

Sahil was a second-year BTech student in the Department of Energy Science and Engineering and was appearing for his third-semester mid-semester examination. The paper was scheduled from 11 am to 1 pm. In its first statement on the incident, an unsigned post published on IIT Bombay’s X account at 3:23 pm on September 19 said Sahil was caught cheating by the invigilator. It said: “Earlier in the day, during the examination, the student was found using a mobile phone in the exam hall. He had uploaded the examination question paper on ChatGPT to seek answers.” The statement added: “No disciplinary action was initiated against the student. The matter was also discussed with the student by the instructor, the faculty adviser and the Head of the Department, who counselled him and assured him that the incident would not adversely affect his academic career.”

This statement followed a protest held by more than 400 students at the main gate of the campus on the night of September 18. After news of Sahil’s death spread on campus that evening, students gathered at the main gate. According to some of them, Sahil was threatened with suspension by the invigilator, Professor Suryanarayan Doolla. There are also contradictory claims about whether Sahil was cheating during the exam. But after he was allegedly asked by Doolla to leave the examination hall, Sahil returned to his hostel, where he was found hanging from the ceiling fan in his room. The Powai police initially took note of the incident as an accidental death.

But after Sahil’s parents arrived in Mumbai on September 19, his father, Ravindra Wakode, alleged that Sahil had faced caste discrimination from Doolla after he cleared his first year. “For the last two months, he has been telling us about Professor Doolla’s behaviour. They have killed my son. The FIR should be lodged against Doolla as well as IIT Bombay director Professor Shirish Kedare,” Sahil’s father said. Accordingly, an FIR against Doolla and others was lodged at the Powai police station, with charges under abetment of suicide and relevant sections of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. Sahil belonged to a Scheduled Caste family from Yavatmal in Vidarbha, Maharashtra. The case has since been transferred to the Mumbai Crime Branch, which is investigating it under ACP Dharmaveer Bansod.

As the students’ protest continued into its third day, September 20, the IIT Bombay administration got into a huddle. The students drew up 18 demands in all, the first being the suspension of Professor Doolla. Meanwhile, the institute’s first statement, which spoke of Sahil cheating during the exam, was also challenged by the students. According to them, Sahil’s All India Rank in the JEE was 614, and his Cumulative Grade Point Average for the first year was 8.5 out of 10, considered a strong score. This raised questions among the students about the statement’s intent.

On the night of September 21, Director Kedare met the protesting students and announced that he was accepting all 18 of their demands. He also promised further talks on September 22. While this was under way, a video surfaced in which Kedare told the students that he too would resign on Monday. But on September 21, IIT Bombay issued a clarification on X saying Kedare had not resigned.

The September 19 statement became a talking point across the country and on social media. Since the FIR carried charges under the Atrocities Act, Sahil’s death quickly turned into a wider caste battle beyond the campus. A section of upper-caste voices sought to build a narrative around IIT Bombay’s September 19 statement, which became a rallying point in the debate. Progressive and Ambedkarite groups, in turn, entered the narrative battle in support of Sahil.

Facing backlash over the statement, IIT Bombay apologised and issued a clarification on September 21, saying: “The details and circumstances leading up to the incident remain subject to investigation by the appropriate authorities. In view of ongoing investigation, it was inappropriate to have set out or characterised details relating to the events preceding his demise before they had been duly established through the appropriate investigative process.” Withdrawal of the September 19 statement had been one of the protesting students’ demands.

Meanwhile, fault lines emerged within the IIT Bombay faculty. After the director accepted the demand to suspend Doolla—who has since been removed from his post as Dean of Student Affairs—a section of faculty members held a march inside the campus in his support. The Faculty Forum issued a statement backing him: “Professor Doolla, the course instructor, was invigilating in the mid-semester examination from 11 am to 1 pm on Friday, 18 September 2026, when he observed that a student was indulging in academic malpractice, viz., unauthorised possession and use of a smartphone during the exam. As part of the institute’s approved procedure, he reported the incident to institute authorities for further action in the matter.” The faculty march followed this statement, with the Faculty Forum reportedly planning to rally all 750 members of the institute’s faculty in solidarity with Doolla.

But Suryakant Waghmare, professor of sociology at IIT Bombay, opposed the Faculty Forum’s position. On X, Waghmare wrote: “Faculty Forum is not a legal body. They are building pressure on the investigation committee. Not all faculty identify with this group.”

Sahil is the third student to die by suicide at IIT Bombay this year, and the tenth across the IITs. Naman Aggarwal, a second-year civil engineering student, died by suicide on February 4. Sohil Rajkumar Sangwan, a materials engineering student, died by suicide on July 28. In 2023, Darshan Solanki, a first-year BTech student, died by suicide, allegedly after jumping from his hostel building. In 2014, Aniket Ambhore, a fourth-year BTech student in electrical engineering, fell to his death from the sixth floor of a hostel; his family has maintained that caste-based humiliation on campus drove him to his death. Ambhore, Solanki, and Wakode all belonged to the Scheduled Caste community.

When Sahil’s father, along with student union leaders and social activists, held a march in Powai on September 21, Ambhore’s and Solanki’s parents joined them. Darshan Solanki’s father, Ramesh, said: “I have come here to support Sahil’s parents. In Darshan’s case, I am sure that the IIT administration or the police are hiding something. I am not satisfied with the investigation that the Mumbai police have done.” Sunita Ambhore, Aniket’s mother, was also part of the protest. “We have been talking about students’ welfare, counselling, and all that. But on the ground, the issues have remained the same. There is academic pressure, but SC and ST students also face another layer of pressure—sometimes even from faculty,” she said.

The Mumbai Crime Branch will investigate the reason for the suicide, but Sahil’s death has already exposed IIT Bombay’s administration to strong criticism from all sides. To address it, the administration has come up with several remedies. Mumbai newspapers have reported that IIT Bombay is considering replacing ceiling fans with wall-mounted ones in hostel rooms. The move has drawn wide criticism on social media, with many users saying that instead of addressing the root cause of the suicides, the institute is offering band-aid solutions.

The suicides of students from marginalised communities at India’s premier higher-education institutions are a widely discussed subject. Between 2014 and 2021, 122 suicides were recorded at the IITs, the IIMs, and Central universities, and 58 per cent of the students involved belonged to the SC, ST, OBC, and minority communities. The figure points to a pattern of discrimination that persists at some of India’s most selective institutions.
If you are experiencing suicidal thoughts, please reach out to a mental health professional or a crisis helpline in your area.
